title: Exploring Radio
description: Amateur radio from first principles — the Canadian certificate exam, antennas, propagation, and getting on the air. Real numbers, no prior knowledge assumed.

items.title: Resonance and Tuned Circuits
items.content_html: Resonance is where a coil's reactance equals a capacitor's. The resonant-frequency formula, series circuits (lowest impedance) versus parallel (highest), bandwidth, and how receivers and antenna traps use it.

items.title: Reactance and Impedance
items.content_html: Reactance in ohms: an inductor's rises with frequency (2πfL), a capacitor's falls (1/2πfC). Why an RF choke and a bypass capacitor stop RF but leave audio alone, and impedance as the total opposition to AC.

items.title: Overview
items.content_html: The Radio Fundamentals articles in reading order: frequency and wavelength, the radio spectrum, decibels, reactance, and resonance, building on the electricity from Exploring Electronics.

items.title: Decibels
items.content_html: Why radio measures gain and loss in decibels: 3 dB doubles power, 10 dB multiplies it by ten, chains of gains and losses add, an S-unit is 6 dB, and antenna gain is quoted in dBi or dBd.

items.title: What Is a Radio Wave?
items.content_html: A radio wave is alternating current set loose from the wire. Frequency and wavelength are one number in two units, wavelength in metres is 300 divided by megahertz, and the ITU's decade bands from VLF to EHF.

items.title: Antennas and Neighbours
items.content_html: The Canadian rules for putting up an amateur antenna (CPC-2-0-03), keeping RF exposure within Safety Code 6, and deciding interference complaints with EMCAB-2.

items.title: Who Enforces the Rules
items.content_html: Where Canada's amateur radio rules come from, what an ISED radio inspector may and may not do, how a certificate can be suspended, and the two routes to a penalty.

items.title: Across Borders
items.content_html: The international rules for Canadian amateurs: the ITU Radio Regulations and regions, third-party traffic, visitors operating in Canada, and operating in the US, CEPT and IARP countries.

items.title: What You May Say
items.content_html: The Canadian rules for what goes over the air: no music, business, secret codes, or payment; who may transmit; sharing bands; emergencies; privacy and penalties.

items.title: Overview
items.content_html: The Getting Licensed articles in reading order: how to get your Canadian amateur radio certificate, then exactly what it lets you transmit under RBR-4.

items.title: What You May Transmit
items.content_html: What a Canadian amateur certificate allows: which bands each qualification may use, maximum bandwidth, power limits, identification, and RBR-4's technical rules.

items.title: Getting Your Certificate
items.content_html: How to get a ham radio licence in Canada: the Basic Qualification exam, what 70% and 80% unlock, finding an examiner, fees, and your call sign. Sourced from ISED.

items.title: The Amateur's Code: Ethics on the Air
items.content_html: The two short codes of conduct that shape amateur radio: Canada's Code of Ethics for Amateur Radio Operators (1997) and The Radio Amateur's Code (1928), and what they look like on the air.

items.title: Start Here
items.content_html: Radio is electricity that changes direction millions of times a second. The electricity you need first, in order, mapped to the Canadian Basic Qualification syllabus.

items.title: ISED Basic Anki Deck
items.content_html: A free Anki deck of all 984 questions in ISED's Basic Qualification question bank, organized by exam section, with notes on what the exam actually draws from it.
